content: CD14, also known as cluster of differentiation 14, is a gene in humans. The protein encoded by this gene plays a critical role in the innate immune system. CD14 exists in two distinct forms: one is membrane-bound (mCD14), anchored to the cell membrane via a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) tail, and the other is a soluble form (sCD14). The soluble form of CD14 can arise either from the shedding of mCD14 (48 kDa) or through direct secretion from intracellular vesicles (56 kDa). Structural studies of CD14 reveal a monomeric, bent solenoid configuration with a hydrophobic amino-terminal pocket. CD14 was the first pattern recognition receptor to be described. It functions as a co-receptor, working alongside Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and MD-2, to detect bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS). However, CD14 can only bind LPS in the presence of lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP). While LPS is considered its primary ligand, CD14 also recognizes other pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), such as lipoteichoic acid. CD14 is predominantly expressed by macrophages and, to a lesser extent (approximately 10-fold lower), by neutrophils. It is also expressed by dendritic cells. The soluble form of CD14 (sCD14) is secreted by the liver and monocytes. Even at low concentrations, sCD14 can enable cells that do not express CD14 to respond to LPS. Both mCD14 and sCD14 are also present on enterocytes. Additionally, sCD14 is found in human milk, where it is thought to regulate microbial growth in the infant gut. CD14+ monocytes have the capacity to differentiate into various cell types, including dendritic cells. This differentiation process is promoted by cytokines such as granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) and interleukin-4 (IL-4). CD14 has been shown to interact with lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), which facilitates its role in recognizing and responding to bacterial components.
